title: Monocular SLAM: assessment on ground truth, then your pool data
subtitle: Gregory German, September 2026. Code, full report and every number: github.com/gregorygerman777-hub/sonar_sim, SLAM/validation/REPORT.md
author: Gregory German

pages.heading: 1. Assessment on datasets with ground truth
paragraphs: As you asked, I first assessed the implementation on data with ground truth, to find bugs before running it on your data: KITTI odometry 00 to 10 (left camera only), plus TUM RGB D, AQUALOC (real underwater video) and a rendered pool scene with exact ground truth, all with the same settings. The SLAM is keyframe based and monocular (tracking against a local map, triangulation, local and global bundle adjustment, relocalization).

Bugs found and fixed. Ground truth exposed two bugs in how the monocular scale is held (the map grew about 2,500 times in local bundle adjustment; map point fusion later collapsed it). A review against the published design the code follows found two more (map points counted and culled wrongly), measurement found a half pixel principal point error in the reference method and the rendered scene, and three errors were in the evaluation metrics. Each is fixed with a test that fails on the old code, and every result here was rerun with the final code.

Results. With SIFT features the SLAM tracks every frame of 10 of the 11 KITTI sequences; with ORB it loses track on 7 and restarts in a new map. Where it tracks every frame, the error is 0.3 % of the distance driven on the short sequences and up to 4.9 % on the long ones, because with no loop closure yet the monocular scale drifts. COLMAP on the same frames: 0.65 m on 04 (mine 1.05 to 1.20 m), 16.98 m on the 07 loop (mine 10.11 to 16.61 m). On the rendered pool scene the 10 m path is recovered to 0.5 cm (ORB) and 0.2 cm (SIFT); on AQUALOC, under 1 cm while it tracks.

pages.heading: 3. Your pool data: trajectory and 3D model from my SLAM
paragraphs: All 117 frames, with your K = [1403.5 0 476.5; 0 1403.5 392.9; 0 0 1]. My SLAM initializes on your stills and tracks 12 consecutive frames, opt28 to opt39, then loses track; over the sequence it starts 4 maps, and none of the others grows beyond 4 frames. The stills are about 2 s apart with large viewpoint changes and moving caustics on the floor, which break frame to frame tracking. Skipping every other frame, or every 2 frames, made it worse (2 frames posed). Below are its two outputs for the longest map, separately and superimposed. Units are arbitrary (monocular).

figures.caption: (d) Estimated camera trajectory, opt28 to opt39: top and side views. Green: first frame, red: last frame.
(e) 3D model: the 635 points of this map.
(f) The trajectory, with a camera frustum at each frame, superimposed on the 3D model.

pages.heading: 4. Your pool data, all 117 frames: trajectory superimposed on the 3D model
paragraphs: To see what your data supports, I also ran a multi view reconstruction (COLMAP: every frame matched against every other, one global bundle adjustment) on the same frames and K. It registers all 117 frames in one model (mean reprojection error 0.92 px). The camera circles the rock and pebble mat about twice at nearly constant height; frames 106 to 117, taken about 10 minutes later, continue on the same circle. Where my SLAM and this model pose the same frames, their relative rotations agree to a median of 0.6 degrees. There is no ground truth, so this is internally consistent, not verified. Units are arbitrary; the floor lane stripes beside the mat measure 0.44 units wide, so their real width would make it metric.

figures.caption: (g) Camera trajectory with frustums, superimposed on the 3D model (12,152 points). The dense patch is the rock and pebble mat; the points above the cameras include reflections in the underside of the moving water surface, which are not physical structure.
(h) The same from directly above the pool floor: points coloured by height, arrows where the camera looks. The trajectory and the model are also attached as data files (.mat, .csv, .ply).
